name: The Pygmalion Effect
statement: Higher expectations placed on people can lift their performance.
meaning: When someone in authority — a teacher, manager, or leader — expects more of a person, that person tends to perform better; when little is expected, they tend to do worse. It is a form of self-fulfilling prophecy: the expectation is not magic, but it changes how the authority figure treats the person, and that changed treatment changes the outcome.
mechanism: Expectations shape the expectation-holder's behaviour toward the target, which shapes the target's performance. Rosenthal grouped the channels into four factors: a warmer emotional climate toward those expected to succeed, more and more challenging input, more opportunities to respond, and more differentiated feedback. Much of this is transmitted subtly, even unconsciously, through tone and body language — overlapping with the way an experimenter's expectations can unconsciously sway results.

examples.text: Rosenthal and Jacobson told teachers that a randomly chosen fifth of pupils were poised to bloom intellectually; by year's end those pupils, especially the youngest, showed larger measured gains than their peers, though the size of that result is disputed.

Dov Eden's field experiments with military trainees found that instructors led to expect more of randomly designated recruits produced higher performance from them, extending the effect to adults at work.
The negative mirror image — low expectations depressing performance — showing the same expectancy mechanism can drag people down as well as lift them up.

variants.name: The self-fulfilling prophecy
variants.text: The broad parent concept, coined by Robert Merton in 1948 — a false definition of a situation that evokes behaviour making the original false conception come true.

variants.name: The golem effect
variants.text: The negative counterpart, in which low expectations lower performance, named for the clay creature of legend that turns destructive.

whyItMatters: It put the power of expectations at the centre of thinking about education, management, and leadership, suggesting that how much we expect of people can shape what they achieve. It launched a large research literature on expectancy effects and remains influential in teaching and organisational practice — even as its founding study and its magnitude are much debated.

working.text: recognise that your beliefs about someone's potential leak into how you treat them and can shape their results.
watch for the golem effect, where writing someone off quietly undermines their performance.
treat expectation effects as real but usually modest and context-dependent, not a reliable lever for dramatic change.

limits: The effect is genuine but modest, inconsistent, and context-dependent, and its founding study is methodologically discredited in important respects. The original IQ instrument was criticised as invalid at the youngest ages, so its dramatic gains may partly reflect regression toward the mean rather than expectancy. Meta-analysis finds small average effects in education, often fading and concentrated in a minority of pupils, while some organisational field experiments report much larger effects — two literatures that should not be conflated. The existence of expectancy effects is supported; their size and generality are disputed.
misreadings: It does not mean expectations reliably transform performance — the effect is usually small and fades, and the striking figures from the original 1968 study should not be taken at face value. And it is named for the Greek myth of the sculptor Pygmalion, whose statue came to life, not simply for the play of the same name.
origin: Introduced by Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson in Pygmalion in the Classroom (1968), from their Oak School experiment; the founding study was sharply criticised by Robert Thorndike, and the broader self-fulfilling prophecy was named by Robert Merton in 1948.
